title: Speaking & Listening
description: Oral communication skills — presentations, discussions, active listening, debating, body language, and adapting speech to audience and purpose.

notes.heading: Preparing and Delivering Presentations
notes.body: A strong presentation: (1) Know your purpose — inform, persuade, entertain? (2) Structure clearly — introduction (hook + roadmap), body (2-3 main points with evidence), conclusion (summarise + strong closing). (3) Use visual aids effectively — slides should SUPPORT, not replace, your speech. Avoid walls of text; use images, keywords, data visualisations. (4) Practice aloud — timing, transitions, difficult words. (5) Engage the audience — eye contact, rhetorical questions, anecdotes, varying tone/pace. (6) Prepare for questions. Delivery tips: Speak slower than feels natural (nerves speed us up). Pause for emphasis — silence is powerful. Vary pitch and volume — monotone loses attention. Stand still (avoid swaying/pacing). Never read verbatim from slides or notes — use bullet points as cues.

illustration.alt: Diagram of a strong presentation: a speaker at a podium flanked by icons for visual aids and audience engagement, above a three-step flow showing introduction (hook and roadmap), body (main points with evidence), and conclusion (summarise and closing).
illustration.caption: A strong presentation follows a clear three-part structure — introduction, body, conclusion — delivered confidently with visual aids that support, not replace, your speech.

notes.heading: Participating in Discussions
notes.body: Effective discussion participation: Listen actively — don't just wait for your turn to speak. Build on others' points: 'I'd like to add to what Maria said...' or 'That's an interesting point, but I wonder if...' Disagree respectfully: 'I see it differently because...' not 'That's wrong.' Encourage quieter voices: 'Sam, what do you think?' Stay focused — don't derail the discussion. Support opinions with evidence or reasoning. Discussion roles: Facilitator (keeps discussion on track, ensures everyone contributes), Note-taker (records key points), Devil's advocate (challenges assumptions — but explain you're doing so). MYP values collaborative discussion — you're assessed on how you engage with others' ideas, not just how well you express your own.

notes.heading: Active Listening Skills
notes.body: Listening is a skill, not passive. Active listening: (1) Give full attention — eye contact, no distractions. (2) Show you're listening — nodding, brief verbal acknowledgments ('mm-hmm,' 'I see'). (3) Paraphrase to check understanding: 'So what you're saying is...' (4) Ask clarifying questions: 'Could you explain what you mean by...?' (5) Avoid interrupting — let the speaker finish. (6) Respond thoughtfully, not reactively. Barriers to listening: rehearsing your response while the other person speaks, judging before hearing fully, filtering (hearing what you expect, not what's said), distraction. In MYP oral assessments, you may be asked to respond to a recording or a peer — demonstrating you've listened carefully is essential.

notes.heading: Debating and Argumentation Skills
notes.body: Debate structure: Motion (the proposition being debated) → Proposition team (argues FOR) → Opposition team (argues AGAINST). Each speaker has a defined role and time limit. Key skills: (1) Constructing arguments — claim + evidence + reasoning. (2) Rebuttal — directly addressing and countering opponents' points (not ignoring them). (3) Point of Information (POI) — brief interjection during opponent's speech to question or challenge (accepted or declined by speaker). (4) Clash — debates are won on the quality of engagement between arguments, not just speech quality. (5) Framing — defining the debate's terms and scope to your advantage. (6) Persuasive delivery — tone, pace, emphasis, body language. In MYP, debating develops critical thinking, quick reasoning, and respectful disagreement.

notes.heading: Non-Verbal Communication
notes.body: Body language communicates as much as words. Eye contact: builds connection and credibility. Avoiding eye contact signals nervousness or dishonesty. Posture: upright, open = confident. Slouched, crossed arms = defensive or uninterested. Gestures: natural gestures emphasise points; excessive/fidgety gestures distract. Facial expression: should match your message — incongruence (smiling while discussing something serious) undermines credibility. Voice: Pace (varied — slow for emphasis, faster for excitement), Volume (project clearly but don't shout), Pitch (vary to avoid monotone), Pause (strategic silence — powerful). Proxemics: use of space — standing still conveys confidence; moving with purpose engages different audience sections. Dress and appearance: appropriate to context. These skills apply to presentations, interviews, discussions, and everyday communication.

notes.heading: Adapting Speech to Audience and Purpose
notes.body: Effective speakers adapt. Consider: Who is the audience? What do they already know? What do they care about? Formal presentation to adults = structured, evidence-based, measured tone. Informal talk to peers = conversational, personal anecdotes, humour. Persuasive speech = rhetorical devices, emotional appeal, call to action. Informative talk = clear structure, examples, avoid jargon (or explain it). Entertaining speech = humour, storytelling, audience interaction. Adapt vocabulary, sentence complexity, examples, and delivery style to the context. A presentation on climate change to scientists uses data and technical language; to primary students uses analogies ('Earth has a fever') and vivid imagery. The mark of a skilled communicator is this adaptability.

notes.heading: Overcoming Communication Anxiety
notes.body: Public speaking anxiety is normal — even experienced speakers feel nerves. Strategies: Preparation is the best anxiety reducer — know your material thoroughly. Practice aloud multiple times, ideally in the actual space. Breathing exercises: slow, deep breaths calm the nervous system. Reframe anxiety as excitement — the physiological sensations are similar (increased heart rate, adrenaline). Focus on your message, not on yourself — you're there to share something valuable, not to be judged. Start strong — a well-rehearsed opening builds confidence. Accept imperfection — audiences rarely notice small mistakes you obsess over. Use notes as safety net, not script. Visualise success. Remember: the audience WANTS you to succeed — they're on your side.

flashcards.definition: Fully concentrating, understanding, and responding thoughtfully — not just hearing words.
flashcards.example: Paraphrasing: 'So what you're saying is...' Asking clarifying questions.

flashcards.definition: Looking at audience members while speaking — builds connection and credibility.
flashcards.example: Scan the room; make brief eye contact with individuals. Don't stare at notes or ceiling.

flashcards.definition: Directly countering an opponent's argument in debate — showing why it's wrong or weaker.
flashcards.example: 'The opposition claims that... However, the evidence actually shows...'

flashcards.definition: Body language, facial expression, gesture, posture, eye contact — communicates alongside or beyond words.
flashcards.example: Crossed arms = defensive. Open palms = honest, open. Leaning forward = engaged.

flashcards.definition: Restating someone's point in your own words to confirm understanding.
flashcards.example: 'So you're arguing that the policy benefits outweigh the costs — is that right?'

flashcards.definition: Defining the terms and scope of the debate to favour your side.
flashcards.example: Debating 'School uniforms should be mandatory' — proposition frames it as 'equity'; opposition frames as 'freedom.'

flashcards.definition: Speed of speaking. Vary for effect — slow for emphasis, faster for urgency.
flashcards.example: Slow down for key points: 'And this... is... the most important thing.'

flashcards.definition: Brief interjection during opponent's debate speech to question or challenge.
flashcards.example: Stand and say 'Point of information.' Speaker can accept ('Yes?') or decline ('No thank you').

flashcards.definition: Deliberately arguing against a position to test its strength — not because you believe it.
flashcards.example: 'Let me play devil's advocate: what if the data is wrong?' — stimulates critical thinking.

flashcards.definition: Slides/images support speech, don't replace it. Minimal text, strong visuals, one idea per slide.
flashcards.example: One striking image + 3 bullet points max. Never read paragraphs from slides.

flashcards.definition: Strategic silence — adds emphasis, allows audience to absorb, controls pace.
flashcards.example: After a key point: 'Education is the answer.' (pause) 'Let me tell you why.'

flashcards.definition: Question seeking to understand better — not challenging, but deepening comprehension.
flashcards.example: 'Could you elaborate on what you meant by 'systemic barriers'?'
